title: Taiwan Stocks Plunge 17% in Worst Week Since 1991 on AI
summary: Taiwan's Taiex tumbles over 17% as Anthropic's IPO fails to lift sentiment, triggering margin calls and forced selling across AI-exposed tech stocks.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Taiwan's Taiex index suffered its worst weekly decline since 1991, dropping over 17% as global AI trade doubts intensified following Anthropic's disappointing market debut.
- The island's Financial Supervisory Commission tightened short-selling restrictions twice in November 2026, capping intraday borrowed-share orders at just 1% of average volume to stabilize markets.
- Forced margin-call liquidations and retail investor deleveraging accelerated losses across Taiwan's tech-heavy benchmark, which has surrendered more than 25% from its October peak.


Taiwan's stock market endured its most severe weekly collapse in 35 years as investor skepticism over artificial intelligence returns triggered a cascading selloff across the island's tech-dominated benchmark. The Taiex index plummeted as much as 6.4% on Friday, November 20, 2026, capping a brutal week that saw total losses exceed 17%, the worst performance since 1991, despite emergency interventions by local regulators to stabilize trading.


## Anthropic IPO Fails to Restore Confidence


The proximate catalyst for Friday's selloff was the underwhelming market reception of Anthropic PBC's blockbuster initial public offering. Shares of the Claude chatbot maker fell 4.7% in after-hours US trading on November 19, 2026, signaling that even a major AI liquidity event could not reverse mounting doubts about whether generative AI investments will deliver commensurate returns. The listing, which many analysts had hoped would reinvigorate the AI trade, instead amplified concerns over the sector's stretched valuations and uncertain profitability timelines.


Steven Leung, executive director at UOB Kay Hian Hong Kong, identified the Anthropic listing disappointment as "the main hit on AI across Asia." With technology stocks commanding over 70% of the Taiex's weighting, the benchmark proved exceptionally vulnerable to any shift in sentiment around AI infrastructure spending and chip demand. Major Taiwan-listed semiconductor manufacturers, which supply critical components to global AI labs, saw their shares battered as investors re-evaluated growth assumptions.


## Regulatory Interventions Prove Insufficient


Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission moved aggressively to stem the bleeding, tightening short-selling curbs for the second time in November 2026. Officially launched on November 20, 2026, the new rules cap intraday borrowed-share orders at just 1% of a stock's trailing 30-day average volume, down from the 3% threshold imposed earlier in the month. Market-making and certain hedging activities received exemptions, but the restrictions marked an escalation of regulatory efforts to prevent speculative pressure from accelerating declines.


Despite these measures, aggregate short interest across Taiwanese equities remained stubbornly elevated at 5.28% of float as of Thursday, only marginally below the 5.49% recorded on November 6 when the first round of restrictions took effect. S3 Partners data suggests short sellers saw little reason to cover positions, anticipating further downside as forced margin liquidations compounded selling pressure. Leung noted that "short sellers are seeing no improvement in downside pressure, so there is no rush to cover their short positions."


## Margin Calls Drive Forced Deleveraging


The speed and severity of the Taiex's decline triggered a wave of margin calls among retail investors, who had been heavily exposed to leveraged positions in AI-linked equities. Barclays analysts wrote in a November 18, 2026 note that forced selling by retail participants was the "main driver" of Monday's brutal session, which ranked as Taiwan's worst single-day selloff in four months. The firm warned that the deleveraging cycle could extend further, creating additional downward pressure on share prices.


The Taiex has now surrendered more than 25% of its value from the record high reached on October 6, 2026, erasing substantial year-to-date gains. The index's 2026 advance has narrowed to approximately 25%, a sharp reversal from the euphoric sentiment that prevailed just weeks earlier when optimism over AI chip demand pushed valuations to historic peaks.


## What This Means


The Taiwan market crash underscores the fragility of equity valuations built on AI infrastructure assumptions. When a marquee event like the Anthropic IPO fails to catalyze a rally, it exposes the depth of investor skepticism about near-term profitability across the generative AI value chain. For Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem, the rout highlights the risks of concentrated exposure to a single thematic trade. Regulators may face difficult questions about whether short-selling restrictions merely delay inevitable repricing or create conditions for more disorderly unwinding once controls are lifted. The coming weeks will test whether the AI trade can stabilize or if further capitulation lies ahead for Asia's tech-heavy benchmarks.
